verification_policy: Every source below was checked for its bibliographic record from a publisher page, a university faculty page, or a reference list. FULL TEXTS WERE NOT READ. VERIFIED_BIBLIOGRAPHIC means the citation exists, not that its findings were reproduced here. PARTIAL means some metadata (book title, editors, page range) is missing. UNVERIFIED means a locator still has to be supplied before the entry may support any link stronger than CANDIDATE. No claim in this file is a finding about any particular lyric.

source_status.VERIFIED_BIBLIOGRAPHIC: citation record confirmed; full text not read; findings not reproduced
source_status.PARTIAL: citation record confirmed but incomplete (missing book editors, page range, or publisher)
source_status.UNVERIFIED: no locator verified in this build; may only back a CANDIDATE link

TERM-REFRAIN.label: refrain
TERM-REFRAIN.definition: A line or short phrase that recurs at recognisable points, often inside or at the end of successive stanzas. Defined by recurrence of material, not by being a separate section.
indicators: same or near-same line reappears at stanza ends
recurrence inside a verse rather than between verses
TERM-REFRAIN.distinguishing_test: Does the recurring material stand as its own section between verses? If yes, prefer TERM-CHORUS. If it is a returning line embedded in a continuing stanza, prefer TERM-REFRAIN.

sources.ref: Britannica, 'incremental repetition' (verse)
sources.access_note: search excerpt retrieved 2026-11-09; full article not read

sources.ref: Music Production Glossary, 'What is a refrain?'
sources.access_note: search excerpt retrieved 2026-11-09; glossary, not peer reviewed

TERM-REFRAIN.claim_limit: A structural label only. It cannot establish listener recall, authorial intent, or emotional effect.

TERM-CHORUS.label: chorus
TERM-CHORUS.definition: A distinct, recurrent section of a song that returns between verses, normally carrying the central theme and a contrast in musical material.
indicators: section boundary separate from the verse
whole section recurs with largely identical text
TERM-CHORUS.distinguishing_test: Is there a separate section boundary in the source, or only a repeated line inside a verse? A repeated line alone is a refrain, not a chorus.

sources.ref: Music Production Glossary, 'What is a refrain?' (refrain vs chorus vs hook table)
sources.access_note: search excerpt retrieved 2026-11-09; glossary, not peer reviewed

TERM-CHORUS.claim_limit: A form label. It says nothing about whether the chorus is memorable to a listener.

TERM-HOOK.label: hook
TERM-HOOK.definition: A memorable, attention-getting fragment (lyric, melodic, rhythmic or timbral) whose function is to be noticed and retained. Functional term: it is defined by a listener response, not by a text pattern alone.
indicators: candidate only until listener evidence exists
TERM-HOOK.distinguishing_test: Is the claim about a feature in the text (refrain/chorus) or about a listener's noticing and recall (hook/INMI)? Only listener data can settle the second.

sources.ref: Byron, T. & O'Regan, J. (2022), 'This Is How We Do It: An Approach to Hooks', Springer chapter
sources.access_note: chapter title, authors, first-online year and DOI confirmed from publisher page 2026-11-09; book title/editors not visible; chapter not read

TERM-HOOK.claim_limit: A text pattern may be a hook CANDIDATE. Without listener data, 'this is a hook' is not an OBSERVED claim.

TERM-INMI.label: involuntary musical imagery (INMI / earworm)
TERM-INMI.definition: A spontaneously recurring musical experience reported by a listener; a phenomenon of the subject, not a property of the score.
TERM-INMI.distinguishing_test: Is there a reported listener experience? A repeated lyric line is not INMI; INMI requires subject-level evidence.

sources.ref: Jakubowski, K., Finkel, S., Stewart, L. & Mullensiefen, D. (2017), 'Dissecting an Earworm: Melodic Features and Song Popularity Predict Involuntary Musical Imagery', Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 11(2), 122-135
sources.locator: journal citation in a published reference list; DOI not confirmed in this build
sources.access_note: bibliographic record confirmed 2026-11-09 via a published reference list; full text not read

sources.ref: Byron, T. P. & Fowles, L. C. (2015), 'Repetition and Recency Increases Involuntary Musical Imagery of Previously Unfamiliar Songs', Psychology of Music, 43(3), 375-389
sources.access_note: citation and DOI confirmed from the Springer chapter reference list 2026-11-09; full text not read

TERM-INMI.claim_limit: The construct belongs to listener experience. A lyric text alone can never make an INMI claim OBSERVED.

TERM-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.label: processing fluency (construct)
TERM-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.definition: The subjective or measured ease with which material is processed; in lyric research it is operationalised through repetition and tested against outcomes.
indicators: repetition count operationalised as an independent variable
a measured outcome such as time-to-chart or recognition
TERM-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.distinguishing_test: Was ease of processing actually measured, or only inferred from a repetition count? Without a measurement it remains a theoretical construct.

sources.ref: Nunes, J. C., Ordanini, A. & Valsesia, F. (2015), 'The Power of Repetition: Repetitive Lyrics in a Song Increase Processing Fluency and Drive Market Success', Journal of Consumer Psychology, 25(2), 187-199
sources.access_note: authors, journal, volume and pages confirmed from University of Washington faculty publication page and a journal reference list 2026-11-09; full text not read

TERM-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.claim_limit: An operationalised construct from a specific study. It does not transfer automatically to a single lyric without a measurement.

TERM-INCREMENTAL-REPETITION.label: incremental repetition
TERM-INCREMENTAL-REPETITION.definition: Repetition of a stanza or line with a small but meaningful variation that advances the content; a recognised device in ballad and verse traditions.
indicators: most lines of a stanza repeat verbatim
the changed line alters the situation, speaker or stakes
TERM-INCREMENTAL-REPETITION.distinguishing_test: Does the changed line advance the situation? If the repetition is only at the start of successive clauses, prefer anaphora; if nothing changes at all, it is plain refrain.

sources.ref: Britannica, 'incremental repetition' (verse)
sources.access_note: search excerpt retrieved 2026-11-09; full article not read

sources.ref: WordReference, 'incremental repetition' dictionary entry
sources.access_note: definition 'repetition, with variation, of a refrain or other part of a poem, esp. a ballad' retrieved 2026-11-09

TERM-INCREMENTAL-REPETITION.claim_limit: A textual device label. It does not by itself establish narrative progression or a listener effect.

TERM-ANAPHORA.label: anaphora
TERM-ANAPHORA.definition: Repetition of a word or expression at the beginning of successive phrases, clauses or verses.
indicators: identical opening words on consecutive lines
TERM-ANAPHORA.distinguishing_test: Is the repeated material at the start of successive clauses (anaphora), or is a whole stanza repeated with one changed line (incremental repetition)?

sources.ref: Merriam-Webster, 'anaphora' dictionary entry
sources.access_note: definition retrieved via search excerpt 2026-11-09; full entry not read

TERM-ANAPHORA.claim_limit: A positional rhetorical label, not an explanation of effect.

TERM-VERSE-CHORUS-FORM.label: verse-chorus form
TERM-VERSE-CHORUS-FORM.definition: A song structure alternating narrative verses with a recurring, contrastive chorus section.
TERM-VERSE-CHORUS-FORM.distinguishing_test: Does the structure contain a separate recurrent chorus, or a 32-bar AABA scheme with a contrasting bridge (B)? Count the sections before labelling.

sources.ref: The Music Theory Professor, 'Understanding Refrain and Chorus Variations in Contemporary Pop Music'
sources.access_note: search excerpt retrieved 2026-11-09; pedagogical source, not peer reviewed

TERM-VERSE-CHORUS-FORM.claim_limit: A form classification under a declared scope; it is not a claim about all songs or about listener response.

TERM-AABA.label: AABA / 32-bar form
TERM-AABA.definition: A four-section scheme with two similar A sections, a contrasting B (bridge), and a return to A.
TERM-AABA.distinguishing_test: Is there a B section with contrasting material? Without a bridge, AABA is not the right label.

sources.ref: UNVERIFIED - a music-theory reference locator is still required

TERM-AABA.claim_limit: Unverified terminology in this ontology; usable only as a named rival, never as a confirmed classification.

TERM-PROSODY.label: prosody / text-setting
TERM-PROSODY.definition: The alignment of linguistic stress, syllable count and phrase shape with musical metre and strong beats.
indicators: strong beats marked in a notation file
function words landing on strong beats
TERM-PROSODY.distinguishing_test: Does the evidence contain scansion or notated beats? Without either, a prosody judgement is an unmeasured reading.

sources.ref: UNVERIFIED - a peer-reviewed or reference locator for text-setting is still required
sources.access_note: not verified in this build; do not use for a link stronger than CANDIDATE

TERM-PROSODY.claim_limit: Unverified terminology in this ontology; a prosody claim without scansion is INTERPRETIVE at most.

TERM-SELF-REFERENCE.label: self-reference / metapoetic device
TERM-SELF-REFERENCE.definition: A lyric passage that refers to the song itself, its own structure, or its own act of being sung.
indicators: the lyric names its own section or device
the text comments on its own repetition
TERM-SELF-REFERENCE.distinguishing_test: Does the line refer to the artefact itself rather than to the narrated situation? State the reading and its rival.

sources.ref: UNVERIFIED - a poetics or narratology locator is still required
sources.access_note: not verified in this build; do not use for a link stronger than CANDIDATE

TERM-SELF-REFERENCE.claim_limit: An interpretive reading. It can never be OBSERVED, and it says nothing about authorial intent.

THEORY-MERE-EXPOSURE.label: mere exposure effect
THEORY-MERE-EXPOSURE.statement: Repeated exposure to a stimulus can increase affective preference for it.
explains: why familiarity can be mistaken for quality
does_not_explain: recall accuracy for a specific lyric
why a writer chose to repeat

sources.ref: Zajonc, R. B. (1968), 'Attitudinal effects of mere exposure', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2), 1-27
sources.access_note: citation and DOI confirmed from the Springer chapter reference list 2026-11-09; full text not read

THEORY-MERE-EXPOSURE.claim_limit: A preference effect, not a memory effect. It cannot turn a text observation into a recall finding.

THEORY-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.label: processing fluency (repetition in lyrics)
THEORY-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.statement: Repetitive lyrics are processed more easily, and that fluency is associated with measurable market outcomes in a corpus of chart hits.
explains: a possible route from textual repetition to ease of processing
why repetition is common in successful songs
does_not_explain: whether this particular lyric is remembered
the effect on a single listener

sources.ref: Nunes, J. C., Ordanini, A. & Valsesia, F. (2015), Journal of Consumer Psychology, 25(2), 187-199
sources.access_note: bibliographic record confirmed 2026-11-09; full text not read; chart-corpus study, not a single-lyric experiment

THEORY-PROCESSING-FLUENCY.claim_limit: A corpus-level association. It licenses a hypothesis about a lyric, never an observation of one.

THEORY-EXPECTANCY-ITPRA.label: musical expectancy / ITPRA
THEORY-EXPECTANCY-ITPRA.statement: Listeners form expectations from learned regularities; imagination, tension, prediction, reaction and appraisal shape the response to confirmation or violation.
explains: why a changed line after repeated lines may be salient
why a return is heard as a return
does_not_explain: whether this writer intended a violation
whether a listener actually felt tension here

THEORY-INMI.statement: Certain melodic features and song-level popularity predict INMI; repetition and recency increase INMI for previously unfamiliar songs.
explains: how repetition and recency relate to earworms

THEORY-WORKING-MEMORY.label: working memory / phonological loop
THEORY-WORKING-MEMORY.statement: A limited-capacity system with a phonological component supports short-term verbal rehearsal.
explains: why short repeated verbal material is rehearsable
does_not_explain: why a particular phrase is preferred

THEORY-REPETITION-IN-POP.label: psychological perspectives on repetition in popular music
THEORY-REPETITION-IN-POP.statement: Repetition in popular music is treated as a multi-function phenomenon requiring psychological, structural and cultural analysis rather than a single mechanism.
explains: why one mechanism name is insufficient for repetition
does_not_explain: which specific function applies to a given lyric without analysis

sources.ref: de Clercq, T. & Margulis, E. H. (2018), 'A Psychological Perspective on Repetition in Popular Music', in O. Julien & C. Levaux (Eds.), Over And Over: Exploring Repetition in Popular Music, pp. 147-161, Bloomsbury

THEORY-REPETITION-IN-POP.claim_limit: A framing source. It explicitly warns against reducing repetition to one mechanism.

THEORY-HOOK-APPROACH.statement: A recent scholarly treatment of hooks as an object of analysis, situating them among repetition and exposure research.

does_not_explain: whether a specific fragment functions as a hook

THEORY-CONCEPTUAL-METAPHOR.label: conceptual metaphor theory
THEORY-CONCEPTUAL-METAPHOR.statement: Metaphor is a cognitive structuring mechanism, not merely a decorative figure of speech.
explains: how a lyric's concrete images can structure an abstract domain
does_not_explain: which mapping a listener actually makes

THEORY-HABITUATION.label: habituation (rival frame)
THEORY-HABITUATION.statement: Repeated stimulation can decrease responsiveness, which competes with a simple 'more repetition is better' reading.
explains: why an exposure account needs a boundary condition
does_not_explain: which regime applies in a given song

sources.ref: Rankin, C. H. et al. (2009), 'Habituation revisited: An updated and revised description of the behavioral characteristics of habituation', Neurobiology of Learning and Memory, 92(2), 135-138
sources.access_note: citation and DOI confirmed from the Springer chapter reference list 2026-11-09; full text not read

THEORY-HABITUATION.claim_limit: A rival explanation. Its presence means a repetition account is CONTESTED, not settled.

relations.note: Repetition is a candidate text feature for the fluency account; no listener measurement here.
Exposure concerns preference, not recall; keep the two effects apart.
The construct is defined by the research programme that studies it.
A changed line after repeated lines is a candidate expectation violation, not an observed one.
Increased preference and decreased responsiveness are rival readings of repetition.
A repeated line is not automatically a separate section.
A song feature is not a listener phenomenon.
